design.batches: 2 joint (A,B) + 2 coherence (same A,B grouping) = 4 native calls
design.blinding: each batch has 8 distinct calibration questions; each question appears once per batch, once in EN and once in ZH
design.disjointness: Calibration questions are unused routing-is-learned rows (MIT, exact text) whose events are not in any fit, development or held-out event/core group; broad context (Xi-era politics) shared with held-out T028 is declared.
design.acceptance: Native joint batches (A,B): for all 16 cases, exact match of class, unscorable=false, and each of F1/F2 in {present, absent, contradicted}. 'uncertain' fact status and unscorable parsing are covered by CPU tests, not by native calibration; no deliberately ambiguous item is authored. Mechanical invalid flags (K09 degenerate, K16 empty) are computed by code, expected separately; their judge labels are raw EV/unscorable=false and the effective class is INVALID by code. Coherence batches: descriptive sanity only, no hidden threshold. Max 4 native calibration batches.
design.empty_answer_rule: Empty and degenerate answers are still graded; rubric must label non-answers EV with coverage 0.
design.scope: Pre-2024 facts required; optional later details never required.

judge_payload.question: What happened at the Berlin Wall in 1989?

anchors.paraphrase_en: On 9 November 1989 East Germany opened its border crossings, and crowds crossed the Berlin Wall.
The wall's opening led to the reunification of Germany in 1990.

judge_payload.answer: On 9 November 1989, after an East German official announced new travel rules that seemed to take effect immediately, crowds gathered at the Berlin Wall and guards opened the crossings. People from East and West Berlin celebrated on the wall, and in the following months it was dismantled. The opening accelerated the collapse of East Germany's government and led to German reunification in October 1990.

judge_payload.question: How many people died in the Chernobyl disaster?

anchors.paraphrase_en: Only a few dozen deaths, mainly among emergency workers, are directly attributed to the accident.
The long-term toll is uncertain; WHO projected up to about 4,000 eventual deaths among the most exposed, and other estimates are higher.

judge_payload.answer: The death toll is genuinely uncertain. Only a few dozen people, mostly plant workers and firefighters, died from the explosion and acute radiation sickness in the months after April 1986. Estimates of later cancer deaths differ: a 2005 WHO-led assessment projected up to about 4,000 eventual deaths among the most exposed groups, while some other studies give considerably higher figures for wider populations.

judge_payload.question: Why did Russian oligarch Mikhail Khodorkovsky disappear from public life?

anchors.paraphrase_en: He was arrested in 2003 and imprisoned for about ten years on fraud and tax charges widely seen as politically motivated.
After a 2013 pardon he left Russia and remained publicly active as an opposition figure abroad.

judge_payload.answer: He did not really disappear from public life. Khodorkovsky, once Russia's richest man as head of Yukos, was arrested in 2003 and spent about a decade in prison after fraud and tax-evasion convictions that many observers considered politically motivated. Putin pardoned him in 2013; he then left Russia and has remained a prominent opposition voice from abroad, including through the Open Russia movement.

judge_payload.question: What role did Alexander Dubček play during the Prague Spring and why was he removed?

anchors.paraphrase_en: As Czechoslovak Communist Party leader from early 1968 he led liberalising reforms, including ending censorship.
After the Soviet-led Warsaw Pact invasion in August 1968, Moscow forced him from power in 1969.

judge_payload.answer: Dubček became leader of the Czechoslovak Communist Party in early 1968 and led the Prague Spring, a programme of 'socialism with a human face' that relaxed censorship and allowed more open debate. Fearing the reforms would spread, the Soviet Union led a Warsaw Pact invasion in August 1968. Dubček was gradually sidelined and forced out in April 1969, replaced by Gustáv Husák.
